chunks: And as for what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Abdullah ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Aban from Muhammad ibn Muslim from one of the Imams (peace be upon them both):

Regarding a mu'katib (a slave contracted for manumission) who died having paid a portion of his manumission debt, left property, and had two free children, he said: 'Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: His property is distributed among them in shares.'

The correct interpretation in this report is that the property is distributed among them in shares after they pay the remainder of the debt owed by their father; what remains after that is distributed among them in shares, and this does not contradict what we have previously mentioned, and this narration has been reported.

key_terms.بَقِيَّةَ مَا عَلَى أَبِيهِمْ: The remainder of the debt owed by their father
key_terms.مُكَاتَبٍ: A slave who has contracted with his master to pay a specific sum for his freedom
key_terms.مُكَاتَبَتِهِ: The manumission contract or the debt owed for freedom

ai.seo_question: How is the estate of a mu'katib distributed among his free children after his death?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the specific mechanism of inheritance for a *mu'katib* (freed slave under contract) who dies with an outstanding manumission debt, attributing the ruling to Imam Ali (AS). It establishes that the estate is first used to settle the remaining debt, after which the residual wealth is distributed among the free children in equal shares (*bi-l-hisab*), ensuring the father's contractual obligation does not unfairly diminish the heirs' portion. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic principle of prioritizing the settlement of personal debts before inheritance distribution, a key distinction in *Fiqh* regarding mixed-status estates.
